newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end lower, jittery ahead of payrolls.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end lower, jittery ahead of payrolls.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed mostly lower on Monday after fresh economic data suggested strength in the manufacturing sector ahead of the release of a key employment report on Friday, analysts said.
The 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended down 12/32 at 97-11/32. Its yield was at 6.83 percent, against 6.80 percent at Friday's close.
"I think people are going to continue to sell upticks ... There is some fear of the employment report," said Lee Youngdahl, vice-president at Aubrey G. Lanston and Co. Inc.

"People have gone into a defensive posture. You've seen some repositioning already but I think you've got some more coming down since the odds of a near-term Fed tightening have gone up substantially," Youngdahl added.

Wall Street pundits said the risks of an interest rate hike have increased after Fed chairman Alan Greenspan said last week he could not rule out a pre-emptive tightening to ward off inflationary pressures.
Players have become wary of a possible rate hike although most economic data released so far point to a continuation of a moderate growth and benign inflation scenario.
"We haven't seen inflation on the radar screens yet," said a trader at a foreign investment bank here. "But some people were a bit concerned about the manufacturing numbers today."

The trader was referring to the release of the National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) index, which rose to 53.1 in February from 52.0 in January. The NAPM prices index rose to 55.1 in February versus 51.4 in January.
Traders expressed concern that a strong NAPM could influence the second leg of Greenspan's Humphrey Hawkins Congressional testimony on March 5. "The market is a bit nervous here," the trader said.

Players were also jittery ahead of the release of the February payroll report on Friday. "I think the data are going to report a strong set of labor conditions," said Joseph Liro, chief-economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
Analysts said the steep back-up in short-term yields over the last few sessions indicated the market is quickly pricing in a possible Fed tightening in the near term.

"I think we're getting very close to fully pricing in at least a 25 basis point move," Liro said, adding he believes the Fed will tighten monetary policy by 25 basis points at the May 20 meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee.
The Fed last changed interest rates in January 1996, when the central bank trimmed the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to the current target of 5.25 percent.

The Treasury market cut some losses in the last part of the trading session as some retailers and speculators covered short positions. But traders said that selling from some Japanese accounts unwinding dollar/yen positions weighed on prices throughout the trading session.
The two-year note ended flat at 99-19/32. Its yield was at 6.09 percent as players returned to the market after the rate pierced the 6.10 percent resistance level earlier in the day.
The yield curve steepened a bit on Monday, with the spread between the two-year note and the 30-year bond widening to 74 basis points from 71 basis points on Friday.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed flat at 5.10 percent. The six-month bill rate was unchanged at 5.17 percent. The year bill rate was up two basis points at 5.38 percent.
The five-year note traded off 2/32 at 99-11/32 to yield 6.41 percent. The ten-year note closed down 3/32 at 97-22/32, yielding 6.57 percent.
